items.question: Should an ASP.NET Core action use Task.Run to call Redis?
items.answer: No. Redis is I/O. await the async API so the request thread returns to the pool. Task.Run would spend a second pool thread waiting on the same I/O and can contribute to starvation under 999 concurrent users. Task.Run is for CPU work you refuse to run on the request path, such as a bounded SkiaSharp raster queued to a Channel.
followUps: What is thread-pool starvation in a blocking Redis client?
items.sixtySeconds: I/O: await. CPU: pool via Task.Run or Parallel. Never Task.Run just to ‘make Redis async.’

items.question: Why is lock(_gate) { await redis.StringGetAsync(...) } forbidden?
items.answer: await yields. The continuation may resume on another thread, so you would Exit on a different thread than Enter — Monitor throws. Even if you block instead of await, every other caller queues behind a network round-trip. Throughput collapses from 199 to 999 users. Compute the cache key and the in-memory check under the lock, then I/O outside, then publish the result with Interlocked or a ConcurrentDictionary.TryAdd.
followUps: What is the C# 13 Lock type’s EnterScope?
items.sixtySeconds: Locks are for CPU-short critical sections. Never await while holding Monitor. Single-flight I/O without holding the lock.

items.question: Is volatile enough for a shared counter of submitted attempts?
items.answer: No. volatile does not make ++ atomic and does not give you a total order Microsoft is willing to call a lock. Two threads can both read 41 and write 42. Use Interlocked.Increment. volatile is a narrow hint against some compiler/hardware reordering for a simple flag; even Microsoft now tells you to prefer Interlocked or lock. long and double cannot be volatile because reads are not atomic on all platforms.
followUps: What does CompareExchange do in a single-flight cache?
How does lock provide a memory barrier?
items.sixtySeconds: Counters: Interlocked. Flags: still prefer Interlocked. volatile is easy to get wrong.

items.question: How do you stop a Redis cache stampede when attempts jump from 199 to 999 concurrent?
items.answer: Do not let every request miss and hit the origin. Use a per-key single-flight: ConcurrentDictionary of Task, or a Channel worker that refreshes. The first waiter starts the Redis/DB fill; the rest await the same Task. Combine with a short lock or Interlocked.CompareExchange only around dictionary mutation, never around the I/O. Add jittered TTL so keys do not expire in lockstep after a deploy.
followUps: How is this different from a Mutex?

items.sixtySeconds: Single-flight per key. Share one Task. Lock only the map, not Redis. Jitter TTLs.
